records.name: Hollyday family (Readbourne and Ratcliffe Manor)
records.scaleNote: Henry Hollyday I (c.1725–1789) held 55 enslaved people in 1776, 77 in 1783 and 131 at death (MSA Biographical Dictionary); his son Henry (1771–1850) held 59 in 1830 and 63 at death (MSA Legacy of Slavery).
records.base: Ratcliffe Manor, near Easton, Talbot County, Maryland
records.origins: James Hollyday Sr. (1696–1747), a deputy naval officer at Oxford, married Sarah Covington, widow of Edward Lloyd, in 1721, tying the family to the Lloyds of Wye. His sons James (1722–1786) built Readbourne in Queen Anne's County and Henry (c.1725–1789) built Ratcliffe Manor near Easton around 1762.
records.role_summary: Eastern Shore tobacco and grain planters whose estates ran on enslaved labour across Talbot, Queen Anne's and Caroline counties. Henry Hollyday I's holdings grew from 55 enslaved people in 1776 to 131 at his death, and his son Henry kept 59–63 people at Ratcliffe until 1850, then left them to be divided among his heirs.

roleDetail.d: Per the MSA Biographical Dictionary, Henry Hollyday I's personal estate of £18,431 included 131 enslaved people; a 1788 codicil gave his son James 18 people at the Readbourne tract.
Henry Hollyday (1771–1850), a Federalist state senator, held 59 people in 1830 and 63 at death; MSA notes he handled escapes privately through slave catchers and informers, not newspaper adverts.
William Green, who fled the neighbouring Goldsborough estate c.1840, accused Hollyday of cruelty in his 1853 narrative; MSA calls this largely uncorroborated.

records.legacy: The family held Ratcliffe Manor for about 140 years and Readbourne from 1730 to 1904; both houses survive as private National Register properties. The Hollyday family papers, including Eastern Shore duty lists on imported 'Negroes', are at the Maryland Center for History and Culture.

legacyDetail.d: Ratcliffe Manor (c.1762) and Readbourne are listed historic houses; the land passed out of the family by the early 20th century.
Hollyday family papers (MCHC) include a volume tabulating 1727–1745 Eastern Shore duties on the importation of enslaved Africans.

records.name: Magruder family (Prince George's and Montgomery)
records.scaleNote: Jeremiah Magruder held 36 enslaved people in 1790 (MSA Biographical Dictionary); Col. Zadok Magruder 26 in 1790 (MCPS); Dr. William B. Magruder 30 in 1860 (MSA Legacy of Slavery); dozens of Magruders appear in the 1867–68 Slave Statistics.
records.base: Prince George's and Montgomery counties, Maryland
records.origins: Alexander Magruder, a Scottish (MacGregor) prisoner of war shipped to the Chesapeake in the 1650s as an indentured servant, became a Calvert County landholder. His descendants spread through Prince George's and Montgomery counties as tobacco planters, justices, tobacco inspectors and militia officers.
records.role_summary: A large planter clan that held enslaved people across several generations. Jeremiah Magruder (1731–1798) held 36 people in 1790; Col. Zadok Magruder of The Ridge near Derwood held 26, placing him in the county's top 4% of enslavers; Dr. William Bowie Magruder held 30 by 1860.

roleDetail.d: Per the MSA Biographical Dictionary, Jeremiah Magruder (36 enslaved, 1790) and a Patuxent tavern-keeper Magruder (15 at death, 1782) were Prince George's justices and tobacco inspectors.
Montgomery County Revolutionary militia colonel; the 1790 census lists 26 enslaved people in his household; a log quarter survives at The Ridge.
Dr. William B. Magruder held 19 people in 1853 and 30 in 1860; one man from his household was drafted into the Union Army in 1864 (MSA).
The Magruder's Landing project traces enslaved people surnamed Semmes, Wright, Crawford, Edmondson and Brown through Magruder wills and the 1867–68 Slave Statistics.

records.legacy: Col. Zadok Magruder High School (Derwood) carries the name; MCPS identified it in 2019 as one of several schools named for enslavers, a renaming petition was accepted in 2023, and the board tabled the change in February 2025 over cost and timing. African American Magruders/McGruders descend from people the family enslaved.

legacyDetail.d: Board tabled Magruder renaming in Feb. 2025 after removing $650,000 from the budget (Bethesda Magazine).
Many Black families in the county carry the Magruder/McGruder name; genealogists link them to Magruder enslavers.

records.name: Beall family (Georgetown, Rockville and Montgomery County)
records.scaleNote: Samuel and Brooke Beall enslaved Yarrow Mamout (c.1752–1796); Upton Beall's widow and daughters bought back 13 enslaved people in 1827 and held 52 by 1860; Margaret Beall received $4,478.50 under DC compensated emancipation in 1862 (Montgomery History).
records.origins: Col. Ninian Beall (d. 1717), a Scottish prisoner turned Maryland militia commander and legislator, patented the 'Rock of Dumbarton' in 1703, the core of later Georgetown. His descendants became planters, sheriffs, merchants and county officials in Frederick, Montgomery and Prince George's counties.
records.role_summary: Planters and town founders whose estates relied on enslaved people. Samuel Beall Jr. bought the West African Muslim Yarrow Mamout; his son Brooke Beall took him to Georgetown and Beall's widow freed him in 1796. In Rockville, Upton Beall's unmarried daughters held 52 people in 1860 and hired some out.

roleDetail.d: Enslaved by Samuel Beall Jr. and then Brooke Beall for about 44 years before his 1796 manumission (Smithsonian NPG).

Upton Beall built the Rockville house c.1815; after his 1827 death his family bought back 13 enslaved people at auction; by 1860 the Beall sisters held 52 people and three quarters (Montgomery History).
Margaret Beall received $4,478.50 under the 1862 DC Compensated Emancipation Act.
No list of people enslaved by the founder has been found; sources document Beall enslavement from his descendants.

records.legacy: The Beall-Dawson House is now Montgomery History's museum and interprets the enslaved household; land Margaret Beall later sold became 'Haiti', Rockville's oldest surviving Black community. Several Beall streets in Montgomery County carry the name; Beallsville is often assumed to be named for the family, but no source found confirms it (the village grew up around the 1748 Monocacy chapel).

legacyDetail.d: Beall-Dawson House (Rockville) run by Montgomery History.
Formerly enslaved people bought lots from Beall land, 1870–1900.
The Montgomery County village is widely linked to the Beall family; no source found states the naming explicitly.

records.name: Worthington family (Anne Arundel, Prince George's and Worthington Valley)
records.scaleNote: Walter B. C. Worthington held 100+ enslaved people at his death in 1845 (per Wikipedia citing family histories); George F. Worthington inherited at least 13 in 1837 (MSA Legacy of Slavery).
records.base: Severn River, Anne Arundel County; Worthington Valley, Baltimore County
records.origins: Capt. John Worthington settled on the Severn in Anne Arundel County in the late 17th century and married into the Ridgely family. Branches spread to Baltimore County, where the family bought so much farmland that the area became known as Worthington Valley, and to Prince George's County.
records.role_summary: Intermarried with the Ridgelys, Brices and Contees, the Worthingtons ran tobacco and grain plantations with enslaved labour. Brice T. B. Worthington lent money to Ridgely kin; Walter B. C. Worthington held more than 100 people on 2,000 acres; George F. Worthington's inherited workers Cinderella (1848) and Eliza Brogdon (1852) escaped from his Severn farm.

roleDetail.d: Owner of 'The Valley' on the old Brookefield tract; at death held 2,000+ acres and 'more than a hundred enslaved people'.
Cinderella fled in 1848 with help from her free husband Abraham Brogden; Eliza Brogdon fled in 1852 (MSA Legacy of Slavery).
Brice T. B. Worthington (1727–1794) married his cousin Anne Ridgely and held a 1770 mortgage on 10,000 acres of his brother-in-law's land (MSA).

records.legacy: Worthington Valley in Baltimore County, now a protected horse-country historic district, carries the name. The family's Baltimore County land records are at the Maryland Center for History and Culture.

legacyDetail.d: MCHC finding aid: the family's early 18th-century settlement established the area known as Worthington Valley.
National Register district including Montmorenci and other Worthington houses.

records.name: Brooke family (Brookefield, Prince George's; Brooke Grove Quakers)
records.scaleNote: Col. Thomas Brooke Jr. (acting governor 1720) left 36 enslaved people in his 1731 inventory (Wikipedia, citing MSA); Quaker Richard Thomas, married to Deborah Brooke, freed about 17 people after rejoining Friends (Preservation Maryland).
records.base: Brookefield, Mattaponi Creek, Prince George's County
records.origins: Robert Brooke arrived in 1650 with his household and was briefly acting governor (1652). His son Maj. Thomas Brooke and grandson Col. Thomas Brooke Jr. built Brookefield on the Patuxent; a Quaker branch (James and Roger Brooke) settled Brooke Grove near Sandy Spring.
records.role_summary: The Anglican/Catholic Brookes of Brookefield held enslaved people as part of a 7,000-acre tobacco estate (36 people in 1731) and intermarried with the Darnalls, Calverts and Taneys. The Quaker branch at Brooke Grove moved toward manumission, but kin such as Richard Thomas Jr. still inherited enslaved people.

roleDetail.d: Thomas Brooke Jr.'s estate inventory listed 36 enslaved people; his stepfather was Col. Henry Darnall.
Brookeville's founder Richard Thomas Jr. enslaved about 16 people in 1790, freed all 17 on rejoining the Quakers, then inherited more (Preservation Maryland).
Chief Justice Roger B. Taney's mother was Monica Brooke of this family.

records.legacy: Brookeville (Montgomery County, founded 1794) is named for Deborah Brooke Thomas's family; Brookefield survives as a place name near Croom. Through Taney the family is tied to the Dred Scott decision.

legacyDetail.d: Town named for the Brooke family by founders Richard and Deborah Brooke Thomas (Town of Brookeville).

records.name: Thomas Bladen (Governor of Maryland, 1742–1747)
records.scaleNote: No record of enslaved people held personally by Bladen was found; his significance is as proprietary governor of a slave colony and as kin of the Board of Trade commissioner Martin Bladen, who sat on Royal African Company business.
records.origins: Born in Annapolis to William Bladen, he was educated in England, became an MP and married Barbara Janssen, sister-in-law of Charles Calvert, 5th Lord Baltimore, who appointed him governor. His uncle Martin Bladen sat on the Board of Trade 1717–1746.
records.role_summary: No documented direct involvement in slavery as an individual owner; as governor (1742–47) he administered a colony whose laws and economy rested on enslaved labour. Bladensburg, created in 1742 as a tobacco port, was named for him.

roleDetail.d: Proprietary governor 1742–1747, dismissed as 'tactless and quarrelsome'.
His unfinished governor's house (begun 1744 on land bought from Stephen Bordley) became McDowell Hall, St. John's College.
His uncle attended 1726 Board of Trade sessions on the 'decay of the trade for negroes' with Royal African Company directors; Bladen County, NC is named for Martin.

records.legacy: Bladensburg, Maryland bears his name; McDowell Hall ('Bladen's Folly') stands at St. John's College. His English fortune passed to daughters who married into the Capell (Earls of Essex) and St John families.

legacyDetail.d: No source found ties Bladen to owning enslaved people; the place name honours a proprietary official, not a planter.

records.name: Hammond family (Howard's Adventure, Gambrills; Hammond-Harwood House)
records.scaleNote: Matthias Hammond held 62 enslaved people in the 1783 assessment (MSA Biographical Dictionary; the museum gives 63) on c.7,800 acres; enslaved men helped build Hammond-Harwood House from 1774.
records.base: Howard's Adventure, Gambrills, Anne Arundel County
records.origins: Charles Hammond (1672–1713) acquired Howard's Adventure through marriage to Hannah Howard; his son Philip (1697–1760), speaker of the Lower House, consolidated it. Philip's sons Matthias, Rezin and others were Annapolis patriots and large planters.
records.role_summary: Tobacco planters whose wealth came from enslaved labour at Gambrills. Matthias Hammond (1740–1786) held 62 people in 1783 and commissioned William Buckland's Annapolis masterpiece, built 1774 by indentured artisans and enslaved men; his brother Rezin held the estate until 1809, when it covered about 9,000 acres.

roleDetail.d: Matthias Hammond's £2,928 assessed property included 62 enslaved people (MSA).
Hammond-Harwood House was raised from 1774 by Buckland's indentured craftsmen and enslaved men, including Buckland's enslaved worker Oxford (museum).
Stones at Howard's Adventure are said locally to have been used for slave auctions; numbers unknown.

records.legacy: Hammond-Harwood House is a museum with a permanent 'Slavery at Hammond-Harwood House' exhibition; Howard's Adventure became a Naval Academy dairy farm in 1913 and the manor burned in 1978.

legacyDetail.d: Hammond-Harwood House Association has run the house as a museum since 1940 and researches the enslaved household.

records.name: Gilmor family (Robert Gilmor & Sons, Baltimore)
records.scaleNote: Documented slaveholding is household-scale: Robert Gilmor Sr. advertised for the runaway Ned (1786); William Gilmor and Robert Gilmor (grandson) held enslaved people in the 1840 census and an 1846 assessment (Natural History Society of Maryland).
records.origins: Robert Gilmor Sr. (1742–1822), a Scottish immigrant, became one of Baltimore's leading Atlantic merchants (Robert Gilmor & Sons) and a city councilman. His son Robert Jr. (1774–1848) was a famous art collector; a grandson built Glen Ellen castle near Towson in 1832.
records.role_summary: A merchant dynasty that held enslaved people in its households and country estate. Records show the runaway Ned (1786), freedom certificates for Sarah (1832) and Ann Barnes (1837), and Levi Cosley, an enslaved man who died in the city jail after an escape attempt in 1840–41.

roleDetail.d: Robert Gilmor Sr. placed an advertisement for Ned, 25.
1840 census and 1846 assessment count enslaved people of William and Robert Gilmor; Levi Cosley's body was retrieved from the Baltimore jail in January 1841.
Robert Gilmor & Sons traded with the West Indies and Europe; no direct slave-voyage involvement has been documented.

records.legacy: Gilmor Street in West Baltimore bears the family name (Gilmor Homes public housing, opened in the 1940s, is probably named after the street, though no source confirming its naming was found). Glen Ellen's ruins lie on Loch Raven Reservoir land.

legacyDetail.d: MSA notes Gilmor Street bears the family's name.
The public-housing project near Gilmor Street is probably named for the street; no source confirming the naming was found.

records.name: William Patterson (Baltimore merchant)
records.scaleNote: Slaveholding is asserted (Wikipedia, unsourced: 'owned several plantations and country estates'; will freed enslaved people at 30) but no census count was found; his account books record 'plantation affairs'.
records.origins: Born in County Donegal, he came to Maryland in 1775 and made a fortune running guns and munitions for the Revolution, then in shipping and banking. He became one of Baltimore's richest men and a founder of the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad.
records.role_summary: A merchant-banker whose fortune came mainly from shipping, not planting; secondary sources say he owned enslaved people on country estates (including Springfield near Sykesville) and that his will freed them at age 30, but this is not yet confirmed by census evidence found here.

roleDetail.d: Wikipedia says he 'was a slave owner' with several plantations and that his will freed his enslaved people at 30 — both unsourced.
His account books at MCHC cover 'plantation affairs' alongside shipping and ground rents.
Revolutionary gun-runner via the West Indies; later a major shipowner and banker.

records.legacy: Patterson Park, Baltimore's 'Best Backyard', began with his 1827 gift of land; Springfield passed to Gov. Frank Brown and became Springfield State Hospital (1896). His daughter Elizabeth Patterson Bonaparte married Napoleon's brother Jérôme.

legacyDetail.d: Established 1827 on land he gave the city.
Grandson Jerome Napoleon Bonaparte; great-grandson Charles Joseph Bonaparte, U.S. Attorney General who created the forerunner of the FBI (1908).

records.name: Franklin Buchanan (Buchanan family, Talbot County)
records.scaleNote: No census count of people he enslaved was found in sources searched; his significance here is marriage into the Lloyds of Wye and the 2023 removal of his name from Naval Academy buildings.
records.origins: Born in Baltimore in 1800 to a prominent Baltimore family, he was a career U.S. Navy officer and in 1845 became the first superintendent of the Naval Academy. In 1835 he married Ann Catherine Lloyd of the Wye House family.
records.role_summary: A Confederate admiral and Eastern Shore planter by marriage. His wife's family, the Lloyds of Wye, enslaved hundreds (Frederick Douglass among them); Buchanan resigned his U.S. commission in 1861 and commanded CSS Virginia and the Confederate squadron at Mobile Bay.

roleDetail.d: Wife Ann Catherine Lloyd; buried in the Wye House family plot. Sources commonly identify her as a daughter of Gov. Edward Lloyd V.
Ranking Confederate admiral; commanded CSS Virginia (1862) and at Mobile Bay (1864).
Not quantified in sources found; Craig Symonds' biography treats slavery as a theme.

records.legacy: The Naval Academy named its superintendent's residence Buchanan House in 1976; in May 2023, following the federal Naming Commission, the Navy renamed it Farragut House, and Buchanan Road was also slated for renaming.

legacyDetail.d: SECNAV renamed Buchanan House as Farragut House (navy.mil).
Three U.S. Navy destroyers were named USS Buchanan.

records.name: Hall family (Anne Arundel and Prince George's planters)
records.scaleNote: Duke's Hall papers (1,020 items, 1736–1862) contain estate inventories listing enslaved people for Maj. Henry Hall (1758), John Hall (1795) and Ruth Hall (1803), and a 1764 overseer contract; counts not published online.
records.origins: Descendants of the Rev. Henry Hall (rector of St James, Anne Arundel, from 1698) became tobacco planters in Anne Arundel and intermarried with Magruders and Snowdens in Prince George's County.
records.role_summary: Tobacco planters who held enslaved people across three generations; their papers document plantation management by overseers, fears of insurrection, and a turn to lumber and wheat after 1800. Francis Magruder Hall Sr. (1786–1826) of Prince George's recorded enslaved family relationships in his will.

roleDetail.d: Estate inventories (1758, 1795, 1803) list enslaved people; a 1764 overseer's contract details plantation management (Duke Rubenstein Library).
The papers include material on slave insurrections.
Francis Magruder Hall Sr.'s will detailed enslaved family ties; kin later filed 1867–68 Slave Statistics claims (Magruder's Landing).

records.legacy: The family papers are at Duke's Rubenstein Library and are used by descendants of the enslaved for genealogy. No named place has been traced to this Hall family.

records.name: Bordley family (Annapolis and Wye Island)
records.scaleNote: John Beale Bordley held 162 enslaved people in Queen Anne's, Talbot and Kent counties in 1783 and 128 in 1790 (MSA); John Wesley Bordley held 57 near Centreville in 1820 (MSA Legacy of Slavery).
records.base: Annapolis; 'The Vineyards', Wye Island, Queen Anne's County
records.origins: Thomas Bordley (c.1683–1726), an English-born lawyer and attorney general, built the Annapolis house now called the Bordley-Randall House. His son Stephen (c.1710–1764) was attorney general and naval officer of Annapolis; his son John Beale Bordley became a judge and agronomist.
records.role_summary: Lawyer-planters whose Wye Island and Eastern Shore estates were worked by enslaved people. John Beale Bordley held 162 people in 1783 even as he wrote that slavery contradicted Lockean equality; he manumitted many or bound them out as apprentices. Another branch, John Wesley Bordley, held 57 in 1820.

roleDetail.d: John Beale Bordley's holdings across three counties (MSA).
Bordley argued slavery made the farmer 'a slave to his slaves' and manumitted many, but still held 128 in 1790.
Stephen Bordley, naval officer of Annapolis 1755–62, trained Samuel Chase and William Paca in law.

records.legacy: Wye Island, divided between Bordley and William Paca through the Chew sisters, was bought by the State of Maryland in the 1970s as the Wye Island Natural Resources Management Area. The Bordley-Randall House stands near State Circle, Annapolis.

legacyDetail.d: State-owned since the mid-1970s (Maryland DNR).

records.name: Belt family (Chevy Chase and Prince George's)
records.scaleNote: Col. Joseph Belt's 1761 will named 28 enslaved people plus others unnamed (Auslander, citing the will); James Beall Belt held 8 in 1860 (Marlboro District slave schedule).
records.base: Chevy Chase tract (Montgomery County / NW Washington)
records.origins: Humphrey Belt reached Jamestown in 1635 and was in Anne Arundel County by 1663. His grandson Col. Joseph Belt (c.1680–1761) patented the 500-acre 'Cheivy Chace' tract from Lord Baltimore in 1725 and held 'Good Luck' in Prince George's.
records.role_summary: Planters in Prince George's, Anne Arundel, Montgomery and DC who passed enslaved people down by will. Joseph Belt divided at least 28 named people (Sango, Batchelor, Nero, Sarah, Juba, Rochester, Hercules and others) among his widow, sons and Sprigg grandsons.

roleDetail.d: Named 28 enslaved people and left others to be divided among grandchildren.
Enslaved people were left for the use of granddaughter Rachel and then grandsons Osborn and Thomas Sprigg.
Belt heirs appear in the 1867–68 Prince George's Slave Statistics.

records.legacy: The name of Belt's 1725 patent, 'Cheivy Chace', is the origin of Chevy Chase, Maryland and DC; the manor house stood at 3734 Oliver Street NW until 1907.

legacyDetail.d: The modern suburb takes its name from Belt's patent, itself named after an English border ballad.

records.name: Duckett family (Melford, Prince George's)
records.scaleNote: Judge Thomas Duckett is described as 'one of the principal slaveholders in the area' (NRHP/Wikipedia); a later Richard Duckett's 36 enslaved people were freed by his administrator at war's end (MSA Legacy of Slavery).
records.base: Melford, near Bowie/Mitchellville, Prince George's County
records.origins: Richard Duckett Sr. (1675–1754) was the first of the name in Maryland. His grandson Thomas Duckett (b.1744) became an associate judge of the Prince George's County Court; Thomas's sons included Dr. Richard Duckett, who built Melford, and Allen Bowie Duckett, a DC circuit judge.
records.role_summary: Tobacco planters and judges. Judge Thomas Duckett presided over several of the Queen family freedom suits, in which descendants of Mary Queen sued for liberty in the 1790s; Melford retains an 18th-century slave quarter.

roleDetail.d: Thomas Duckett presided when Queen family freedom suits went to trial in Prince George's (Early Washington DC Law & Family project).
Three-bay gable-roofed slave quarter, probably 18th century, on the NRHP-listed site.
Daniel Clarke, administrator for Richard Duckett (c.1831–1864), freed his 36 enslaved people (MSA).

records.legacy: Melford stands on the grounds of the Maryland Science and Technology Center in Bowie; the house and slave quarter are on the National Register (1988).

legacyDetail.d: Home of Ducketts and Hardestys for 140 years.

records.name: Waring family (Mount Pleasant, Upper Marlboro)
records.scaleNote: Freedom certificates (1812, 1819) name people raised in the family of Basil Waring; John Henry Waring of the 4th District filed claims for people such as Sophy Lane and Matilda Henson in the 1867–68 Slave Statistics (MSA).
records.base: Mount Pleasant, near Upper Marlboro, Prince George's County
records.origins: Basil Waring of Calvert County (d. 1688) left Patuxent tracts to his sons; Marsham Waring inherited Mount Pleasant from his grandfather in 1713, and John Waring built the present house between 1764 and 1785.
records.role_summary: Patuxent tobacco planters who held enslaved people from the colonial era to emancipation. Eleanor Waring manumitted some by deed in 1812; in 1867–68 John Henry Waring sought compensation for people freed in 1864.

roleDetail.d: Certificates of freedom record people raised in Basil Waring's family freed by Eleanor Waring's 1812 deed (MSA).
John Henry Waring filed 1867–68 Slave Statistics declarations (MSA index).
Anna Maria Waring of Germantown held 6 people in 1860 (MSA).

records.legacy: Mount Pleasant (Upper Marlboro) survives as a historic house. No public naming beyond the house name has been traced.

legacyDetail.d: Waring family seat, house built 1764–1785; John Waring buried there (1813).

records.name: Joseph S. Donovan
records.scaleNote: Historian Jonathan Pritchett counts 395 people in eight shipments 1845–47; 93 more sailed on the John C. Calhoun in 1850; Bancroft found 144 shipped 1851–52 (per Wikipedia). 1860 census: $350,000 in property.
records.origins: Born in Baltimore in 1800, Donovan ran the Vauxhall Garden tavern in the 1830s and served on the city council in 1840 before entering the slave trade around 1840 from Light Street.
records.role_summary: One of Baltimore's largest interstate slave traders. He bought Austin Woolfolk's Pratt Street jail in 1843, moved to 13 Camden Street in 1846 and to Eutaw and Camden near the B&O station in 1858, shipping people by sea to New Orleans traders such as J. M. Wilson.

roleDetail.d: Light St (c.1840–42), Pratt & Cove (1843–47), 13 Camden (1846–58), Eutaw & Camden (1858–61) (Baltimore Heritage).
Hundreds of people shipped to New Orleans; manifests survive for 1845–52.
Shipped the family of White House coachman William Williams (1850) and bought James Hamlet after his 1850 Fugitive Slave Act recapture.

records.legacy: His widow Caroline Donovan gave $100,000 in 1889 to found Johns Hopkins University's first endowed chair; in 2023 the university resolved to remove her name and petitioned a Baltimore court. His Green Mount Cemetery vault survives.

legacyDetail.d: JHU Name Review Board recommended de-naming the Caroline Donovan Professorship; approved by trustees in Oct. 2023 pending court approval.
Baltimore Heritage marks the jail sites, though nothing physical remains.

lineage.name: Austin Woolfolk
lineage.note: Sold his Pratt Street jail to Donovan in 1843.

lineage.name: Joseph S. Donovan
lineage.note: Slave trader.

lineage.name: Caroline Donovan
lineage.note: Inherited c.$2m; endowed JHU chair; no children.

records.today: The Donovans had no children; Caroline Donovan's estate went to nieces, nephews and charities. No publicly documented descendants have been traced.

records.name: James F. Purvis
records.scaleNote: Franklin & Armfield's Maryland agent c.1831–42; e.g. 57 people shipped from Richmond on the Orleans (1838) and 59 people to New Orleans in four lots (1840) (per Wikipedia citing manifests).
records.origins: Born in Tennessee to slave trader Allen Purvis and Margaret Franklin, sister of Isaac Franklin, he was sent to Baltimore around 1831 to set up Franklin & Armfield's operation there.
records.role_summary: Ran a Baltimore slave jail on Harford Avenue and agents at hotels near the B&O depot, buying Chesapeake people for sale in Natchez and New Orleans. In 1842 he announced he had quit the trade after converting to Methodism and turned to banking (Purvis & Co.; president of Howard Bank).

roleDetail.d: One of the firm's five major agents c.1833–34.
57 people on the Orleans (1838); 59 in four lots (1840).
Slave-trade capital moved into Purvis & Co. (c.1844–1868) and Howard Bank.

records.legacy: Purvis's bank failed in 1868; he died a farmer in Carroll County in 1880 and is buried at Green Mount. Baltimore Heritage marks the site of his slave pen.

legacyDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage 'Site of the Purvis Slave Pen'.

records.name: Henry family (Weston, Dorchester County; Gov. John Henry)
records.scaleNote: Kinsman Isaac Henry held 22 enslaved people in 1783 (MSA Biographical Dictionary); Gov. John Henry left 4,226+ acres but his personal estate and enslaved holdings are unrecorded in sources found.
records.origins: Descendants of the Presbyterian minister Rev. John Henry of Somerset County. John Henry Sr. (c.1714–1781) was a Dorchester legislator; his son John Henry (1750–1798) was a Continental Congressman, one of Maryland's first U.S. senators and governor 1797–98.
records.role_summary: Eastern Shore landholders in a slaveholding society. Direct holdings at Weston are not quantified in the sources found; kin Isaac Henry held 22 enslaved people in 1783 and 15 at death, and Gov. Henry married Margaret Campbell, granddaughter of the Goldsboroughs.

roleDetail.d: Isaac Henry (m. Dorothy, daughter of John Henry Sr.) held 22 enslaved people in 1783 (MSA).
Governor Henry held at least 4,226 acres in Somerset, Dorchester and Caroline at death; enslaved labour is probable but unquantified.

records.legacy: Gov. Henry was reburied at Christ Church, Cambridge, in 1908. No major public place has been traced as named for him in Maryland.

legacyDetail.d: Slaveholding of the governor himself is not documented in the sources searched.

records.name: Yarrow Mamout
records.scaleNote: Two portraits (Charles Willson Peale, 1819; James Alexander Simpson, 1822), Georgetown deeds, and a 2015 archaeological dig at his Dent Place home document his life.
records.origins: A literate West African Muslim (born in Guinea, per the Smithsonian), he was captured as a young man and shipped to Annapolis around 1752, where Samuel Beall Jr. bought him.
records.role_summary: Enslaved for about 44 years by Samuel Beall Jr. and his son Brooke Beall, first near Potomac and after 1788 in Georgetown, where he made bricks and worked as a labourer. Beall's widow freed him in 1796; he bought a house on Dent Place, invested in Columbia Bank stock and was painted by Charles Willson Peale in 1819.

roleDetail.d: Bought by Samuel Beall Jr.; inherited by Brooke Beall (Smithsonian NPG).
Freed 1796 at about 60; owned property in Georgetown and kept his Muslim faith openly.

records.legacy: His Simpson portrait (DC Public Library) and Peale portrait (Philadelphia Museum of Art) are among the earliest portraits of an African Muslim in America; James H. Johnston's book 'From Slave Ship to Harvard' traces his relatives and descendants.

legacyDetail.d: Dent Place site excavated in 2015.

records.name: Hammond-Harwood House (Annapolis)
records.description: Five-part Georgian house begun 1774 for Matthias Hammond by William Buckland's crews of indentured artisans and enslaved men, including Buckland's enslaved worker Oxford. From 1811 to 1864 the Loockerman family enslaved up to seven people there (Mary, Matilda, Juliet, Harry and others); a museum since 1940 with a permanent slavery exhibition.

records.name: Ratcliffe Manor (Talbot County)
records.description: Georgian plantation house near Easton completed c.1762 by Henry Hollyday and held by the family for about 140 years. Henry Hollyday (1771–1850) held 59 enslaved people there in 1830 and 63 at his death (MSA).

records.name: Beall-Dawson House (Rockville)
records.description: Built c.1815 by Upton Beall, clerk of the Montgomery County court. His widow and daughters bought back 13 enslaved people at his 1827 estate sale and held 52 by 1860; now the headquarters museum of Montgomery History.

records.name: Melford and its slave quarter (Bowie)
records.description: Duckett family plantation house (rebuilt c.1810 by Dr. Richard Duckett) with a three-bay gable-roofed slave quarter probably of the 18th century; listed on the National Register in 1988 and now within the Maryland Science and Technology Center.

records.name: Caroline Donovan Professorship (Johns Hopkins)
records.description: Johns Hopkins' first endowed chair, created by Caroline Donovan's $100,000 gift of 1889 from the fortune of her husband, slave trader Joseph S. Donovan. In October 2023 the university's Name Review Board recommended removing her name, the president and trustees agreed, and JHU petitioned Baltimore City Circuit Court because of the gift's terms.

events.title: Ninian Beall patents Rock of Dumbarton
events.text: The Scottish militia commander takes up 795 acres on the Potomac that become the core of Georgetown; his descendants later enslave Yarrow Mamout there.

events.title: Joseph Belt patents 'Cheivy Chace'
events.text: Lord Baltimore grants Col. Joseph Belt the tract that gives Chevy Chase its name; his 1761 will divides at least 28 named enslaved people among his heirs.

source.label: Mark Auslander — Enslaved persons from Chevy Chase

events.title: Bladensburg named for Gov. Thomas Bladen
events.text: Garrison's Landing, a new tobacco port on the Anacostia, is renamed for the incoming proprietary governor.

events.title: Enslaved men begin building Hammond-Harwood House
events.text: Matthias Hammond, who held 62 enslaved people by 1783, commissions William Buckland, whose crews include indentured artisans and enslaved men such as Oxford.

events.title: Maryland tax assessment counts Eastern Shore and Annapolis enslavers
events.text: John Beale Bordley is assessed for 162 enslaved people, Henry Hollyday for 77 and Matthias Hammond for 62.

events.title: Yarrow Mamout freed in Georgetown
events.text: After about 44 years enslaved by the Bealls, Yarrow Mamout is freed by Brooke Beall's widow and becomes a Georgetown property owner.

events.title: Donovan takes over Woolfolk's Pratt Street jail
events.text: Joseph S. Donovan buys Austin Woolfolk's jail and ships about 395 people to New Orleans in 1845–47 alone.

events.title: Cinderella escapes the Worthington farm
events.text: Helped by her free husband Abraham Brogden, Cinderella flees George F. Worthington's farm near Round Bay; Eliza Brogdon follows in 1852.

events.title: Hopkins de-names Donovan chair; Navy renames Buchanan House
events.text: Johns Hopkins moves to strip Caroline Donovan's name from its first endowed chair, and the Navy renames the Naval Academy's Buchanan House as Farragut House.

events.title: Magruder High School renaming tabled
events.text: Montgomery County's school board postpones renaming Col. Zadok Magruder High School, named for a man who held 26 enslaved people in 1790.

source.label: Bethesda Magazine — Board tables Magruder renaming
